newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia to kickstart delayed mass privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Croatia to kickstart delayed mass privatisation.

text.p: Croatia expects to kickstart a long-delayed mass privatisation scheme this week by announcing a list of state assets for distribution among some 350,000 beneficiaries, a senior privatisation official said on Tuesday.

Assistant Privatisation Minister Damir Ostovic said the move follows months of deliberations to choose the best companies out of what remains in the no longer thick or very valuable portfolio of the state privatisation agency.

"We will probably have the list ready by Friday," Ostovic told Reuters in an interview. "The government is committed to offering top quality assets, that is what gives credibility to the voucher scheme."

The list has been closely guarded, stirring speculation in recent months as to what firms will be included as the Croatian Privatisation Fund swapped holdings with banks and two state pension funds in preparation for the scheme.

The proposed operation, designed to get rid of some four billion German marks ($2.3 billion) worth of state holdings and help develop the fledgling capital market, was approved by a privatisation law that is now almost one year old.

But apart from companies, the authorities also needed time to draw up tentative lists of people who will get free vouchers and prepare a media campaign to explain the procedure, Ostovic said. The scheme may take up to mid-1998 to complete.
It will give beneficiaries, mostly displaced from Serb-held areas of Croatia and other victims of the 1991-95 war, five months from April to register at some 20 regional centres.
Afterwards, probably in the autumn, the government will distribute certificates which will then be exchanged for actual shares in individual firms through three auction rounds.
However, those hoping to get hold of the most attractive stocks like Pliva pharmaceuticals in exchange for free vouchers may be disappointed, Ostovic said.
He withheld names of any companies, saying only that the most likely candidates included hotels and some of the country's leading electrical, textile and food businesses.
The interest for particular shares would determine their initial price in relation to vouchers, and the process would be repeated at a lower value until the supply was exhausted.
"The value (of shares) on offer will exceed 'nominal rights' to give leeway for manoeuvres in case of stronger demand," Ostovic added.

He said businesses in formerly occupied areas would be handed over without competition to their ex-employees and other residents who had to flee those regions when the Serb-Croat war broke out six years ago.

Once the scheme is completed, the state agency will have little left of the assets disposed of when the government first started privatising the economy in 1991 through employee buyouts and selected direct sell-offs to foreigners.
All utilities were nationalised at the time. Banks and other strategic sectors such as shipbuilding were also exempt then and will only come up for sale in the next three years.

While the government has to go through with mass privatisation to attract key votes in this year's elections as well as international aid, experts seem less convinced that it will significantly boost the economy.

They doubt that new owners with very poor management experience and even thinner resources will be able to bring back to life industrial facilities or hotels, some of which have been closed for several years.
"What is needed to help economy is hefty cash investment, but it has to be done now," said one analyst who asked not to be named
"The impact will be felt more in giving birth to investment funds and developing the culture of investing."
